big: Dadi has ₹1 lakh she will not need for five years. A company needs money to build a factory. What if she lent it, and the company paid her interest for using it?

lines: Beta, is a bond the same as a fixed deposit? The agent used both words.
Close cousins, Dadi. Both are loans. Let us follow ₹1 lakh lent for five years and see what comes back.

intro: A company issues a bond with a face value of ₹100 and an 8% coupon, ending in 10 years.
note: The coupon is fixed on the face value when the bond is issued. It does not change with the price you pay later.

alt: Bars showing interest adding up each year until the principal returns
caps: Dadi lends ₹1 lakh at a 7% coupon.
Every year she receives ₹7,000 in interest.
After five years the interest paid adds up to ₹35,000.
On the last day the ₹1 lakh principal is returned too.
Total back: ₹1.35 lakh. That is what lending means.

q: Meena lends ₹1 lakh through a bond with a 7% coupon for 5 years. What does she receive in total over the five years?
opts: ₹7,000 in total, because the coupon is paid only once at the end
₹35,000 of interest across the years, plus the ₹1 lakh back at the end
₹1.07 lakh at the end, since interest is added once at maturity
₹35,000 and no principal, since interest replaces the repayment
why: The coupon is paid every year, not once. Over five years it adds up to much more than ₹7,000.
Seven percent of ₹1 lakh is ₹7,000 a year, so ₹35,000 over five years, then the principal returns.
Interest is paid each year on the bond, not added in a single step at the end of the term.
Interest is on top of the repayment. The borrower still returns the principal at maturity.

q: A bond with an 8% coupon and ₹100 face value is bought today for ₹95. What does the 8% refer to?
opts: 8% of the ₹95 paid, since that is the money the buyer actually gave
A rate that changes every year to follow the bank's savings rate
The total return across the whole life of the bond to maturity
8% of the face value of ₹100 each year, whatever price is paid
why: The coupon is set on the face value, not on the price a later buyer pays in the market.
The coupon is fixed when the bond is issued. It does not float with savings rates.
Eight percent is a yearly rate. Over many years the total is far larger than 8%.
The coupon is a fixed 8% of face value, ₹8 a year for each ₹100, however much you paid.

q: Dadi asks how a bond differs from a fixed deposit. Which answer is correct?
opts: A bond is a tradable loan from a company or government
A bond is a share in the company, so Dadi would share its profits
A bond pays no interest at all, while a deposit always pays interest
A bond is insured by the bank up to ₹5 lakh, while a deposit is not
why: A bond is a loan certificate that can often be sold, issued by companies or governments.
A bond is a loan, not ownership. Lenders get interest, not a share of profits.
Bonds pay interest, called the coupon. That is the main reason people buy them.
Deposit insurance covers bank deposits, not bonds. The reverse of this claim is closer to true.

q: On the maturity date of a 10-year bond, what should the borrower do?
opts: Start paying double interest to reward holders who waited for ten years
Offer new units at a lower price to the people who lent earlier
Return the principal, along with the final interest payment that is due
Cancel the bond and keep the principal as a fee for the loan
why: Nothing doubles at maturity. The bond simply ends and the loan is repaid.
Bonds do not issue units. That wording belongs to mutual funds, and it is not part of repayment.
Maturity is when the loan ends: the final interest is paid and the principal comes back.
Keeping the principal would be a default. A borrower must repay it on the maturity date.

pts: A bond is a loan you give, and the borrower pays interest and returns the principal.
The coupon is a fixed rate set on the face value at the start.
Maturity is the date the loan ends and the principal comes back.
